# Erdős-Herzog-Piranian Conjecture

The Erdős-Herzog-Piranian conjecture asserts that, among all monic polynomials Image: p(z) of a fixed positive polynomial degree Image: n with complex coefficients, the level curve Image: |p(z)|=1 has greatest arc length when Image: p(z)=z^n-1 (Erdős et al. 1958). The level curve is taken in the complex plane.

Tao (2025) proved the conjecture for all sufficiently large Image: n. The conjecture for every polynomial degree remains open (Bloom 2026).

This is problem 114 in the Erdős problems collection (Bloom 2026).

## Problem #114 — Erdős–Herzog–Piranian Lemniscate Conjecture

Statement: Among all monic polynomials of degree n, the lemniscate {z ∈ ℂ : |p(z)| = 1} has maximal arc length when p(z) = zⁿ − 1.

Prize: $250 · Status: Open for small n (solved for sufficiently large n by Tao, Dec 2025)

### Background

  * n = 2: Proved by Eremenko–Hayman (1999), who also showed a maximizer exists with all critical points on the lemniscate
  * n ≥ N₀: Proved by Tao (arXiv:2512.12455, Dec 2025) with a tower-exponential threshold N₀
  * n = 3–14: Certified computationally in this repository (Mendoza, 2026)
  * n = 15: In computation (Modal clusters proposed)
  * n = 16–18: Open but computationally feasible via distributed architectures
  * n = 19 to N₀: Open, beyond current hardware

The maximal length of the Erdős–Herzog–Piranian lemniscate in high degree

15 December, 2025 in math.CV, paper | Tags: Erdos, lemniscate, polynomials | by Terence Tao | 19 comments

I’ve just uploaded to the arXiv my preprint The maximal length of the Erdős–Herzog–Piranian lemniscate in high degree. This paper resolves (in the asymptotic regime of sufficiently high degree) an old question about the polynomial lemniscates

∂E₁(p) := { z : |p(z)| = 1 }

attached to monic polynomials p of a given degree n, and specifically the question of bounding the arclength ℓ(∂E₁(p)) of such lemniscates. For

I recently explored this problem with the optimization tool AlphaEvolve, where I found that when I assigned this tool the task of optimizing ℓ(∂E₁(p)) for a given degree n, that the tool rapidly converged to choosing p to be equal to p₀ (up to the rotation and translation symmetries of the problem). This suggested to me that the conjecture was true for all n, though of course this was far from a rigorous proof. AlphaEvolve also provided some useful visualization code for these lemniscates which I have incorporated into the paper (and this blog post), and which helped build my intuition for this problem; I view this sort of “vibe-coded visualization” as another practical use-case of present-day AI tools.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * Same author earlier posted a 72-page preprint on Quillen’s local parameter conjecture in dimension four (arXiv 2610.13469), listed in the 2026-10-09 catalogue

## What happened

Yunpeng Li of the School of Data Science at CUHK Shenzhen posted a short paper (v1 on Oct 10, 2026, revised Oct 14) that answers the second question of Erdős Problem #1117. For an entire function f that is not a monomial, let ν_f(r) count the points on the circle |z| = r where |f| reaches its maximum. Herzog and Piranian showed in 1968 that ν_f(r) can be unbounded along some radii. Erdős’s second question, whether a single function can have ν_f(r) → ∞ on all large circles, stayed open. Li shows the answer is no: the count is bounded by 2k, where k is the gap between the first two nonzero Taylor terms of f, except on a locally finite set of radii, and the bound is sharp.

The paper’s closing disclosure says ChatGPT and Codex running GPT-6 were used “to develop the proof and prepare the manuscript”. It does not say which steps the models found.

## Why it matters

It is another decades-old Erdős question (the list carries Hayman’s 1967/1974 problem-book provenance) answered in a preprint whose author credits a GPT-6 model with developing the proof. As with most such claims this month, it is unrefereed and erdosproblems.com has not yet updated the problem’s status.
